opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things are going to matter a lot.

The first is just whether we can keep building tasks that are long enough. The whole metric depends on having a suite of tasks spanning a range of human completion times, and as models get better, the frontier of what's interesting keeps moving out. If models are succeeding at, say, fifty percent on tasks that take a skilled human a full day or a week, you need a decent number of tasks in that range and beyond, and you need human baselines for them. Baselining multi-day or multi-week tasks is expensive, it's noisy, and it's hard to find people with the right expertise who'll sit down and actually do the thing under controlled conditions. So a lot of it is practical: can we scale the benchmark construction fast enough to keep the top of the distribution meaningfully above where models are?

The second is whether the relationship between task length and difficulty stays as clean as it has been. Part of why time horizon has worked is that, empirically, human time-to-complete has been a pretty good single-dimensional proxy for how hard a task is for models. That's somewhat surprising, and there's no guarantee it holds. You could imagine models getting very good at long tasks that are long because there's a lot of straightforward work, while still struggling on shorter tasks that require some particular kind of insight or taste or messy real-world context. If the fit to that logistic curve starts getting worse, if success stops being well predicted by length, the single number starts hiding more than it reveals.

Related to that is the distribution question. Our tasks are mostly software and research engineering style tasks, fairly well-specified, with automatic or at least clear scoring. Real work is often much messier: underspecified goals, needing to coordinate with people, long feedback loops. We've seen some evidence that performance is lower on messier tasks. So whether time horizon stays useful partly depends on whether trends on our clean tasks keep tracking what's happening on messier, more realistic ones, or whether those diverge.

Then there's measurement and scoring itself. As tasks get longer, verifying that a model actually did the task well, rather than gaming the scorer or producing something that looks right, gets harder. Reward hacking-like behavior is something we already have to watch for, and with longer, more open-ended tasks that gets worse. If we can't trust the scores, the metric's not worth much.

And finally, I think there's a question of interpretation. Even if the measurement stays sound, people need to understand what it means. A fifty percent time horizon of some number of hours doesn't mean a model can replace a person for that many hours of work in general. If the number gets used as a kind of headline without that context, it could become less useful as a communication tool even while it's still a decent research measure.

So, my overall take: I think it'll stay useful for a while, especially as a way of putting different models and different eras on a common, interpretable scale. But I'd expect that over the next year or two we'll need to supplement it, with messier tasks, with better ways of measuring reliability rather than just fifty percent success, and probably with more direct measures of real-world impact, to keep it honest.

r001.rationale: The response says that baselining multi-day or multi-week tasks is expensive and requires people with the right expertise to complete them under controlled conditions, identifying a practical cost constraint.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of things. The first one is just whether the tasks we're measuring on continue to be representative of the things people actually care about. The way the time horizon metric works is you take a bunch of tasks, you get human baselines for how long they take, and then you look at what length of task the model can do with, say, 50% reliability. And that's a really nice, interpretable number. But it depends a lot on the task distribution. Right now, a lot of the tasks are software engineering and ML research-ish tasks, because that's what we can measure well and it's what we care about for things like AI R&D automation. If models get really good at those specifically, in a way that doesn't generalize to messier, more open-ended work, then you could see the number keep going up while the thing it's supposed to be a proxy for doesn't move as much.

The second thing is just whether we can keep producing tasks at the right difficulty level fast enough. The trend has been doubling every few months, and that means the tasks that were hard a year ago are now easy. So you need tasks that take humans days or weeks, and those are expensive to build and expensive to baseline. If we run out of good long tasks, the metric kind of saturates, not because the models stopped improving but because we can't measure it anymore. And at that point you start getting a lot of noise at the top end, and people will reasonably ask whether a reported horizon of a month means anything.

And then the third thing, which I think is maybe underrated, is the human baseline side. The whole metric is anchored to how long a human takes, and for long tasks that gets really fuzzy. Which human? With what context? Do they get to ask questions? So as the horizons get longer, the uncertainty in the denominator gets bigger, and I think that's going to be the thing that determines whether people trust the number. If we can get a decent story there, I think it stays useful. If not, I'd expect it to get replaced by something more domain-specific.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks lasting days or weeks are expensive to baseline, identifying the cost of establishing human completion times for increasingly long tasks as a measurement constraint.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot depends on whether longer tasks continue to expose limitations that are meaningfully different from the limitations we see on shorter tasks. Can a model keep track of what it’s doing, notice when it’s made a mistake, and recover without someone stepping in? If improvements on those things translate into being able to complete longer tasks reliably, then time horizon seems like a useful way to summarize progress.

The thing I’d be cautious about is treating task duration as if it were itself a measure of difficulty. Something can take a human a long time because it’s repetitive, or because it requires a lot of judgment, and those might look very different to an AI. So I’d want to see whether the trend holds across different kinds of tasks, and whether it predicts success on new tasks outside the benchmark.

And reliability matters quite a bit. Being able to do a long task half the time is interesting, but it’s a different capability from being able to delegate that task and trust that it will get done. If the time horizon is increasing at higher levels of reliability too, I’d find that substantially more informative.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human intervention and task reliability, but does not identify the cost of paying humans to complete increasingly long tasks as a constraint on estimating AI time horizons.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot depends on whether we can keep measuring it on tasks that are representative of the things we actually want AI systems to do. The appealing thing about time horizon is that it gives us a way to talk about progress in terms of the length of tasks a system can complete, rather than just its score on a particular benchmark. But human task duration isn’t a complete description of difficulty. A task that takes someone several hours might involve a lot of repetitive work, or it might involve one really difficult judgment.

So I’d want to see whether the trend holds as we add new tasks, vary the kinds of work we’re measuring, and look at different levels of reliability. Being able to complete a long task half the time is interesting, but for many applications you need much higher reliability. If improvements in measured time horizon also predict that systems can reliably take on longer pieces of real work, then I think it remains a useful metric. If the number keeps going up but that connection gets weaker, we should put less weight on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task duration, task variety, and reliability, but does not identify the cost of paying humans to complete increasingly long tasks as a practical constraint.
